pr_title: FileSystem.AccessControl tests not cleaning files properly
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/44766

The TempDirectory helper class is disposable. The finalizer calls a function that deletes the folders left behind, without throwing exceptions on fail.

This protective try catch hid some additional errors that were not caught when these unit tests were first written, so I'm fixing them:

- I created a class that inherits from TempDirectory to override the folder deleting method
- In the finalizer, I iterate through all the files and folders created by the test, ensure their ACLs give me full control (in case the tests prevent deletion), then attempt to delete the tree.
- To verify my changes, I did not put the finalizer code in a try catch, so I could see the errors thrown when attempting to delete the tree.
- The deletion exceptions helped me find that GetAccessControl needs to be called with the AccessControlSections.Access argument, otherwise they throw "PrivilegeNotHeldException: The process does not possess the 'SeSecurityPrivilege' privilege which is required for this operation."
- I avoided creating files and directories using a FileSecurity or DirectorySecurity that did not have its access rules defined. Files and folders created this way could not be deleted.
- I avoided testing AccessControlType.Deny. This would also cause deletion exceptions.
- Moved some repeated code into common methods.
- Before commiting, I made sure to put the file/folder deletion code inside a try catch to prevent finalizer exceptions.
pr_comments: Thank you, @danmosemsft for your suggestion to look inside the TempDirectory dispose/finalizer code.

The last commit has the `try` `catch` commented in the `DeleteDirectory` method: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/47074/commits/ed557006266e3754ba423ac6e4fb4d620316433d

When the CI finishes successfully, I'll uncomment the `try` `catch` and merge.

All checks passed for commit https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/47074/commits/ed557006266e3754ba423ac6e4fb4d620316433d with the try catch commented.
I'm submitted another commit bringing back the try catch so that I can merge.

> _Can you please run the code coverage report and verify that it is not being regressed by this change?_

@Jozkee @adamsitnik 

I compared before and after my changes (making sure I had the same commit as the baseline for both runs).

There is a ~1% reduction in code coverage in the System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl unit tests. I needed to remove some `FileSystemRights` combinations (and make sure they all had a `Read`) to ensure the files would still be deletable.

We trust your judgement as the engineering owner of this area. Whether or not we should, we've not (except maybe in JSON) applied a hard rule - or even been consistent about measuring it. My inclination would be: the most important thing is whether something significant has been left uncovered, than reaching a particular number.

The unit test failures are unrelated to my change:

- System.Net.Tests.HttpWebRequestTest_Sync.ReadWriteTimeout_CancelsResponse

    - Libraries Test Run release coreclr Linux x64 Debug

- ThreadPoolBoundHandleTests.MultipleOperationsOverSingleHandle_CompletedWorkItemCountTest
    - Libraries Test Run release coreclr windows x86 Debug

@Jozkee @adamsitnik I submitted a new commit where I address your suggestions:

- I brought back the unit tests that consumed the parameterless `FileSecurity` and `DirectorySecurity` constructors. The files and dirs were being created in a way that `DeleteDirectory` was unable to _enumerate_ so that I could reset their permissions before deleting them.
- I made sure to avoid _enumerating_ files and folders in `DeleteDirectory` because that action expects access permission. Instead, any files or folders that a unit test creates, are passed to lists in the `TempAclDirectory` class. If non empty, they get traversed so the files and dirs they contain get their permissions restored (no need to enumerate if I already know what to modify).
- I brought back all the `FileSystemRights` in the inline data of some tests. I added comments describing why some of them cannot be tested.

I ran all these tests with the `try` and `catch` in `DeleteDirectory` commented, to make sure nothing was throwing in the finalizer.

issue_context.title: System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl tests leave behind files ACL'ed to be difficult to delete
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl/tests/FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.cs#L475

In checking out some helix machines, I found various leftovers from these tests, some of which result in creating files and directories which are specific deny-acl'ed for all users.  

Ideally any changes done like this could be cleaned up via a finally() block, since if a real user runs these tests locally their personal temp folder could be clogged up with the same.
comments:
This could potentially be done in TempDirectory itself -- when it fails to do the delete it attempts to fix the ACL's recursively
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1923bba394c31bc2d4f62a948eac8dbe64339ab2/src/libraries/Common/tests/System/IO/TempDirectory.cs#L46

That way it would help all tests that use it.

review_comments: Why didn't you passed `AccessControlSections.Access` in this case?

All the `GetAccessControl` methods that do not take an `AccessControlSections` argument, call that other overload internally. This is how I thought we could get code coverage for both overloads.

<details>
  <summary>DirectoryInfo</summary>
 
 https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1d9e50cb4735df46d3de0cee5791e97295eaf588/src/libraries/System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl/src/System/IO/FileSystemAclExtensions.cs#L13-L21
</details>

<details>
  <summary>FileInfo</summary>
  https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1d9e50cb4735df46d3de0cee5791e97295eaf588/src/libraries/System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl/src/System/IO/FileSystemAclExtensions.cs#L44-L52
</details>

<details>
  <summary>FileStream</summary>
 
 https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/1d9e50cb4735df46d3de0cee5791e97295eaf588/src/libraries/System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl/src/System/IO/FileSystemAclExtensions.cs#L87-L101
</details>
For this specific method (the one that receives a FileStream) there is no overload that takes AccessControlSections.
If this method is already called inside a try-catch block, why is it needed to add another one?
In case of failure here, I want the forloop to continue with the rest of the files and folders. Without this try catch, the larger one would capture the exception and the forloop would exit.
Seems like these two tests are still missing.
I improved this test and renamed it to DirectoryInfo_Create_MultipleAddAccessRules.
What about DirectorySecurity_CreateDirectory_DefaultDirectorySecurity?
Seems like DirectorySecurity_CreateDirectory_DefaultDirectorySecurity is testing the same as DirectoryInfo_Create_DefaultDirectorySecurity. How odd.
In the existing test cases, when would this comment be true?
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/47074#discussion_r569899563
Why is this assertion being removed?

I should've created a duplicate test where the DirectorySecurity is created without constructor parameters, and another one where I pass full control. The former would fail with unauthorized, the latter would not fail.
Seems like you are merging this test with `DirectorySecurity_CreateDirectory_DirectorySecurityWithSpecificAccessRule`. Can you keep them separate or is there any reason for that?
My mistake. The name of this test should be `DirectorySecurity_CreateDirectory_DirectoryAlreadyExists`.
Seems that this test is being removed, is that ok?
I discovered that the unit tests that called the parameter-less `*Security()` constructors, would create undeletable files/folders.

This is the error I get when I comment the dispose try catch and run this unit test:

```
 System.IO.FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.DirectoryInfo_Create_DefaultDirectorySecurity [FAIL]
        System.UnauthorizedAccessException : Access to the path 'C:\Users\carlos\AppData\Local\Temp\jciofg25.azp\createMe' is denied.
        Stack Trace:
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\System.IO.FileSystem\src\System\IO\Enumeration\FileSystemEnumerator.Win32.cs(87,0): at System.IO.Enumeration.FileSystemEnumerator`1.CreateRelativeDirectoryHandle(ReadOnlySpan`1 relativePath, String fullPath)
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\System.IO.FileSystem\src\System\IO\Enumeration\FileSystemEnumerator.Windows.cs(168,0): at System.IO.Enumeration.FileSystemEnumerator`1.MoveNext()
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl\tests\TempAclDirectory.cs(24,0): at System.IO.TempAclDirectory.DeleteDirectory()
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\Common\tests\System\IO\TempDirectory.cs(38,0): at System.IO.TempDirectory.Dispose()
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl\tests\FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.cs(457,0): at System.IO.FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.Verify_DirectorySecurity_CreateDirectory(DirectorySecurity expectedSecurity)
          D:\runtime\src\libraries\System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl\tests\FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.cs(206,0): at System.IO.FileSystemAclExtensionsTests.DirectoryInfo_Create_DefaultDirectorySecurity()
    Finished:    System.IO.FileSystem.AccessControl.Tests
```

@carlossanlop are you also getting this error after fixing https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/47074/files#r568284892 ? We can do some brain storming and find a way to fix it somehow, it would be a pitty to remove a test because the CI does not know how to remove a temp file.

I brought it back. I discovered that the problem was in the way I was attempting to reset the permissions in all created files and folders before deleting them. I changed the logic in DeleteDirectory.
Do we still have sufficient coverage of all these somewhere?

There are other unit test files in this assembly that verify other `FileSystemRights` are correctly set.
Maybe I should bring back _some_ of the InlineData combinations. I noticed some combinations were either not accepted or would prevent me from deleting files. I think anyth rights involving `Read`, `Write` or `Execute` in any combination should probably be ok.

So the only `FileSystemRights` I could bring back to the `InlineData` would be those that have a `Read` flag. Otherwise, the `DeleteDirectory` method we call when disposing will fail to enumerate the folders. Makes sense.
I brought back all the ones I had deleted.
Same questions as above.
Brought them back.
